Abstract

Reconstructing the geological history of the Amazon River and its palaeo-drainage is of prime importance for understanding the control of tectonics and geodynamics processes on Amazonian landscape dynamics and the origin of Amazonian biodiversity. In this study, we report new stratigraphic, sedimentological and provenance constraints on the Neogene sedimentary rocks of the Madre de Dios Basin (South Peru). Our multidisciplinary dataset shows that the Neogene sedimentary rocks of the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (12.5–13° lat S) have a different provenance than those of the southern part (13–14° lat S). The sedimentary rocks of the northern part of the basin are characterized by Solimoes-like ƐNd (0) values (between −9.8 and −5.2) for fined grained sedimentary rocks, REE signatures suggestive of authigenic Fe-oxides formed from sulfide oxidation processes and U–Pb age distributions dominated by zircon ages between 0.9–1.3 Ga (Grenville/Sunsas), 0.5–0.7 Ga (Brasilian/ Pampean), 290–252 Ma (Permian magmatism) and, to a lesser extent, zircon ages younger than 130 Ma (Andean Arc). We interpret the source of these sedimentary rocks to be the Altiplano and the Eastern Cordillera (EC). In contrast, the Neogene sedimentary rocks of the southern part were sourced from the EC and Sub-Andean Zone (SAZ) with secondary Fe-oxides derived from silicate rock weathering. Combined with previous studies, these contrasted geochemical signatures imply the existence of a palaeogeographic barrier within the Madre de Dios Basin between the Cretaceous and the Pliocene suggesting that the southern limit of the Amazonian palaeo-drainage basin was located within the Madre de Dios Basin.

## 1. Introduction

The Amazon River is the largest supplier of materials to the world’s oceans, providing about 20% of the global water (Callède et al. 2004), ~10% of the dissolved load (Gaillardet et al. 2003) and ~3% of the suspended load (Milliman and Syvitski, 1992). The Andean Amazonian rivers are dominant contributors transporting more than 95% of the mean annual suspended sediment flux delivered (2/3 and 1/3 from the Solimões and Madeira rivers, respectively, see Figure 1a for location (Filizola and Guyot, 2004). The geological history of the Amazon’s palaeo-drainage is the result of the interaction of geodynamic mechanisms (acting within the South American plate) with climate and sea-level fluctuations (Sacek et al. 2023). Recent studies have shown the existence of continent-wide cratonic palaeo-drainage originated in the Amazon craton between the Cenomanian and the Maastrichtian in western Amazonia (Hurtado et al. 2018; Rodrigues et al. 2023). Western Amazonia started to be sourced by the Andes between the late Maastrichtian and the Palaeocene (Hurtado et al. 2018; Louterbach et al. 2018b); whereas the eastern Amazonian palaeo-drainage of the Palaeogene had cratonic provenance (Stewart et al. 2016; van Soelen et al. 2017). The Neogene configuration of the Amazonian palaeo-drainage still remains debated (Roddaz et al. 2005; Hoorn et al. 2010; Roddaz et al. 2011; Albert et al. 2018; Hoorn et al. 2017; van Soelen et al. 2017; Sacek et al. 2023; ). Most previous studies focused on the timing of the onset of the transcontinental Amazon River (Figueiredo et al. 2009; Gorini et al. 2014; Hoorn et al. 2017; van Soelen et al. 2017) and its driving mechanism (e.g. Andean mountain building, flat-slab subduction or dynamic topography; Shephard et al. 2010; Eakin et al. 2014; Sacek, 2014; Rodríguez Tribaldos et al. 2017; Bicudo et al. 2019, 2020).The Neogene geological history of the western Amazonian palaeo-drainage is less constrained but viewed as similar in all western Amazonian basins (Roddaz et al. 2011). These basins (Figure 1b) were part of an unique Amazonian retroarc foreland basin (Roddaz et al. 2011) fed by Andean rivers

After the demise of the Pebas megawetland and the end of the Acre Phase in the Late Miocene (Hoorn et al. 2010), the Pliocene uplift of the Fitzcarrald Arch separated the Solimoes from the Madeira drainage basins (see Figure 1a for location, Espurt et al. 2007, 2011a; Roddaz et al. 2011). The tropical Andes and the adjacent Amazon Basin are the world’s most biodiverse regions (Rahbek et al. 2019; Hoorn et al. 2022). The present-day biodiversity of the Amazon region inherited from the Neogene and Andean mountain building, which was the main factor for the evolution of Amazonian landscapes and ecosystems (Hoorn et al. 2010). Within the Amazon Basin, major tributaries and their drainage dynamics represent tectonically driven river captures (Albert et al. 2021). The landscape dynamics caused by topographic barrier migration are suspected to have played a major role in the diversification of Amazonian vertebrates since the Neogene (Ribas et al. 2011;

Oberdorff et al. 2019; Albert et al. 2021) and, even, since the Palaeogene (Musher et al. 2022; Cassemiro et al. 2023). Hence, constraining the Neogene history of western Amazonian palaeodrainage is not only important for understanding the Andean uplift but may also provide important temporal milestones for understanding the origin of the Amazonian biodiversity. In this study, we provide new stratigraphic constraints, seismic interpretations (based on the interpretation of a new subsurface seismic dataset), sedimentological sections, major and trace element geochemistry, Sr–Nd isotopes and U–Pb detrital zircon ages on the Neogene sedimentary deposits of the Salvaci´on syncline of the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (South Peru), one of the widest biodiversity hot spots in Amazonia (Torre-Marin Rando et al. 2021). We revise the Neogene stratigraphy of the Salvaci´on syncline and determine the provenance of the Neogene sedimentary rocks. 2. Geological setting

2.a. Structural setting

The Madre de Dios Basin is located between 12º and 14º S latitudes in the south-eastern part of the Peruvian Andes and Amazonian Basin (Figures 1 and 2). The Madre de Dios Basin comprises the Madre de Dios Sub-Andean Zone (SAZ) and the Madre de Dios foredeep and is included in the southern Amazonian retroarc foreland basin (Roddaz et al. 2005). The SAZ is separated from the Eastern Cordillera (EC) by the Azulmayo thrust, named ‘Main thrust’ in Perez et al. (2016) and from the Madre de Dios foredeep by the Tambopata thrust, which corresponds to the Sub-Andean thrust front (Figures 2 and 3). The Madre de Dios foredeep is limited by the Brazilian Shield to the north and northeast and the Fitzcarrald Arch to the north and northwest. In the northern part of the Madre de Dios area (Pongo de Co˜neq area, Figures 2 and 3), the piggy-back basin (Salvaci´on syncline) is transported by the Sub-Andean thrust front (Louterbach et al. 2014; Perez et al. 2016). The Salvaci´on syncline comprises Late Cretaceous- Cenozoic marine, tide-influenced and fluvial deposits (Gil Rodriguez, 2001, 2002; Louterbach et al. 2014). In the southern part of the Madre de Dios area (Inambari area, Figures 2 and 3, Moizinho et al. 2023), the Punquiri piggy-back syncline is also transported eastward by the Sub-Andean thrust front, termed

Tambopata thrust (Baby et al. 2018a, b). The strata involved in the Punquiri syncline are Paleogene to Pleistocene in age (Louterbach, 2014; Baby et al. 2018a, b; Moizinho et al. 2023).

2.b. Stratigraphy of the Madre de Dios Basin

The Cenozoic sedimentary infill of the Madre de Dios Basin comprises approximately 3.3 km of siliciclastic sediments (Gil Rodriguez, 2002; Louterbach, 2014; Moizinho et al. 2023). The detailed stratigraphic record of both the SAZ and foredeep depozones can be found elsewhere (i.e. Gil Rodriguez, 2001; Hermoza, 2004; Roddaz et al. 2011). The sedimentary succession of the SAZ consists of the sedimentary rocks of the Palaeocene Huayabamba Formation, the Miocene Ipururo Group and the Plio-Pleistocene Mazuko Formation. The Huayabamba Formation and the Ipururo Group are present in the foredeep but the Plio- Pleistocene Mazuko Formation is absent. The stratigraphic ages of the Cenozoic sedimentary succession are supported by palynological data (Valdivia, 1974; Caldas and Kehrer, 1982; Gutierrez, 1982; Carpenter and Berumen, 1999), thermochronological analysis (Hermoza, 2004) and radiometry (40Ar/39Ar dating, Campbell et al. 2001; Gil Rodriguez, 2001; Moizinho et al. 2023). The Palaeocene Huayabamba Formation consists of estuarine tidedominated sedimentary rocks of Andean origin (Louterbach et al. 2014, 2018b). The Ipururo Group of the SAZ consists of three formations: the Bala Formation, Quendeque Formation and Charqui Formation (Roddaz et al. 2011). The deposits in these formations are predominantly fluvial to alluvial (Gil Rodriguez, 2001, 2002; Hermoza, 2004; Roddaz et al. 2011) although some coastal facies have been recognized in the Bolivian Quendeque

The Neogene sedimentary infill of the Punquiri syncline may be divided into two sedimentary sequences (Moizinho et al. 2023). This facies association is comprises siltstones and mudstones overbank deposits and is interpreted as fluvial channel-fill deposits (Moizinho et al. 2023). The second sequence consists of clast supported conglomerates with a medium to coarse-grained arkosic sandstone fining upward to sandstones matrix. This facies developed on an erosive surface and is associated with mudstones and siltstones overbank deposits. The facies association of the second sequence represents braided river deposits (Moizinho et al. 2023). Growth strata deposits are observed in the Late Miocene-Pleistocene sediments of the Punquiri syncline (Louterbach, 2014; Moizinho et al. 2023). The sedimentation rates calculated using the Petromod 1D software show a twofold increase from the Early-Middle Miocene (212.8– 118.2 m/Ma) to the Late Miocene-Quaternary (381.1–354.4 m/Ma, Louterbach, 2014). The facies description and facies association of the Neogene sedimentary infill of the Salvaci´on syncline are available in Louterbach (2014). Three depositional sequences were interpreted from the Neogene sedimentary infill of the Salvaci´on syncline. The first depositional sequence is Early to Middle Miocene in age and consists of well-developed paleosols and laterally migrating sandy bars interpreted as meandering fluvial deposits (Marivaux et al. 2012) and fluvial sandy channels associated with fine grained overbank sediments deposited by a fluvial system under a monsoon-like tropical climate (Antoine et al. 2013). The second depositional sequence is Late Miocene-Early Pliocene in age (Louterbach, 2014). It consists of isolated sandy to conglomeratic channels finning upward to siltstones and abundant overbank deposits including fine laminated mudstones and siltstones and paleosols. It is interpreted as deposited in either a large floodplain across in which the channel meandered or a rapid floodplain aggradation rate relative to the frequency of channel avulsion (Louterbach, 2014). The third depositional sequence is Late Pliocene to Pleistocene in age. It is composed of thick vertically stacked conglomerates deposited by braided streams in proximal fluvial/alluvial environment (Louterbach, 2014). Growth strata deposits are observed in the Late Miocene-Pliocene sediments of the Salvaci´on syncline (Louterbach, 2014). Similary to Punquiri syncline, the sedimentation rates calculated using the Petromod 1D software show a twofold increase from the Early-Middle Miocene (119.98–146.2 m/Ma) to the Late Miocene-Quaternary (359.2.1–344.6 m/Ma, Louterbach, 2014).

2.d. Biostratigraphic constraints and seismic stratigraphic correlations

The stratigraphic dating of the Salvaci´on syncline (Pongo de Co˜neq area) is based on published studies (Marivaux et al. 2012; Antoine et al. 2013; Louterbach et al. 2014), which described Palaeogene and Neogene outcrops. Three seismic sections, imaging the Pongo de Co˜neq SAZ and Madre de Dios foredeep (seismic lines Hepc- 09-02, Hepc-09-01 and 96MGLP101), were used to make correlations within the Salvaci´on syncline. The seismic facies were identified in the Cenozoic infill, based on amplitude characteristics and correlated with the Cariyacu-1X well, seismic sections (Hepc- 09-01 and Hepc-09-02). The definition of seismic facies and seismic correlations within the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin was made by Mélanie Louterbach during her PhD thesis (Louterbach, 2014). The stratigraphic dating of the Punquiri can be found in Moizinho et al. (2023). However, it was impossible to correlate the

results obtained in the Salvaci´on syncline (Louterbach, 2014) to those recently published of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (Moizinho et al. 2023). This is because the axis of the Punquiri syncline is offset to the north with respect to that of the Salvaci´on syncline and almost no along-strike fault correlation can be made between the Pongo de Coneq and Inambari area (Figure 2). A possible explanation for the impossibility of seismic and fault correlations could be the presence of unmapped transfer fault or other structures located between the two area, potentially between 71°00 0 and 70°30 0 where the Tampobata thrust front is offset to the north in the Punquiri syncline (Figure 3).

2.e. Neogene deformation and erosion of the Eastern Cordillera (EC) and Subandean zone (SAZ)

The deformation and erosion of the southern Peruvian Amazonian thrust wedge, which include the EC and SAZ of the Madre de Dios Basin, have been the subject of numerous studies. Based on the construction of balanced-cross sections associated with thermochronology ages and provenance data, Perez et al. (2016) suggested that the EC started to deform and exhume in the Eocene with the reactivation of Triassic normal fault. A Paleogene age of onset of deformation is also proposed by Baby et al. (2018a, 2018b) based on the identification in seismic lines of growth strata deposits associated with the reactivation of Permo-Triassic normal fault. Following this Paleogene period, the northern Bolivian and southern Peruvian Amazonian EC and SAZ experimented significant deformation and erosion during the Neogene in response to the interplay of Climatic and Tectonics processes (McQuarrie et al. 2008; Louterbach et al. 2018a; Baby et al. 2018b; Falkowski et al. 2023; Moizinho et al. 2023). Wet climate is advocated to limit the propagation of deformation within the wedge between ca 19 and 8 Ma (McQuarrie et al. 2008) and favoured the development of passive roof duplexes combined with other tectonics and lithological processes (Mora et al. 2014). Tectonics-induced deformation favoured the propagation of the SAZ towards the craton, topographic growth and out of sequence thrusting of the EC since the Late Miocene (Baby et al. 2018a, b; Falkowski et al. 2023; Moizinho et al. 2023). Occurrence of Pliocene (U–Th)/He ages across the EC is interpreted as indicating widespread Pliocene incision of the southern Peruvian and Bolivian EC in response to precipitation changes induced by sea surface temperature changes during the global transition from early Pliocene warmth to late Pliocene cooling (Lease and Ehlers, 2013). However, evidences of Pliocene growth strata deposits in the SAZ suggest that deformation is also a driver for the Pliocene erosion recorded in the EC and SAZ of the Madre de Dios Basin (Louterbach, 2014; Moizinho et al. 2023). Paleoelevation models suggest that the Aycacucho region (72–76° longitudes W and 13–15° latitudes S) reached modern elevation as early as 22 Ma and that other parts of the southern Peruvian EC gained 1.5–2 km of elevation between 25 and 10 Ma (Sundell et al. 2019). Following these models, modern elevation of the Altiplano and EC adjacent to the Madre de Dios Basin is attained at ca 10 Ma (Sundell et al. 2019).

Major and trace element concentrations were measured at the Service d’Analyse des Roches et Mineraux (SARM, INSU facility, Vandoeuvre-Les-Nancy, France) by ICP- OES (Na, Mg, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, Mn, Fe, Al, Si and P) and ICP-MS (Rb, Cs, Ba, Sr, Th, U, Y, Zr, Nb, Hf, Cr, V, Co, Cu, Ni, Zn, La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Sm, Eu, Gd, Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, Yb, Lu and Ta) after alkaline fusion. 3.b.2. Labile sedimentary Fe-oxides The rare earth element (REE) composition of extractable Fe-oxide phases (e.g., ferrihydrite, lepidocrocite) leached from sediments can provide additional constraints for distinguishing bedrock lithology and weathering processes in modern river basins (Bayon et al. 2020; Jang et al. 2024). Given the well-defined lithological contrasts within the Madre de Dios Basin (Figure 3), we applied this new approach by analysing Fe-oxide leachates from ten sediment samples from the northern Pongo de Coneq section (n = 4) and the southern Inambari section (n = 6) (Supplementary Fig. S2, Table S1). For a detailed tectono-stratigraphic evolution discussion for the Inambari, the reader is referred to Moizinho et al. (2023). Bulk sediment samples were first sieved to obtain the <63 μm fraction and then subjected to a stepwise leaching protocol following the method described by Bayon et al. (2002). Carbonates were initially removed using 5% acetic acid (AA). Subsequently, easily reducible iron oxyhydroxides – such as ferrihydrite and lepidocrocite – were extracted using a mixture of 15% AA and 0.05 M hydroxylamine hydrochloride (HH). The leachate was then filtered through a 0.20 μm membrane, evaporated at 120°C for 24 hours, redissolved in nitric acid to eliminate residual HH, evaporated again at 110°C and finally dissolved in 4 M hydrochloric acid. Major and trace element abundances were determined at the Pôle Spectrométrie Océan (Brest, France) using a Thermo Scientific Element XR sector field (SF) ICP-MS operated in lowresolution mode. Elemental concentrations were calculated using the Tm addition method, following procedures outlined by Barrat et al. (1996) and Barrat et al. (2012). To assess the precision and accuracy of our data, a series of certified reference materials (BCR- 2, DNC-1, GSPN-2, GSPN-3 and GSMC-3) were analysed. The precision for major and trace elements was better than 3 %, and the accuracy of measured concentrations was typically <5 %. The REE

concentrations are reported relative to the initial mass of bulk sediment and were normalized to values for the PAAS (Pourmand et al. 2012), denoted by the subscript ‘N’.

3.c. U–Pb dating

Five Neogene sandstones were collected from river outcrops along the Salvaci´on syncline (see Figures 2 and 3 and Table S1 for locations), and one modern sand sample was obtained at Puerto Maldonado to determine their U–Pb zircon age distribution (see Table S1 for locations). Details regarding the LA-ICP-MS U–Th– Pb dating of the analysed samples at the Laboratory of Geochronology of the University of Brasilia (Brazil) can be found in the supplementary information and in Table S2 (supplementary dataset). In short, to ensure data quality, U–Pb age measurements were screened by excluding zircon grains with the following characteristics: (1) elevated 204Pb values; (2) large uncertainties in isotopic ratios (greater than 3%); and (3) discordance exceeding 10% calculated as (1-(206Pb/238U age/207Pb/205Pb age))*100. All resulting data are available in Supplementary Table 2 the 206Pb/ 238U ratio for grains younger than 1.0 Ga and the 206Pb/207Pb ratio for those older than 1.0 Ga, following the approach of Nemchin and Cawood (2005). To statistically compare the detrital age distributions of the analysed samples, we used the standard multidimensional scaling (MDS) statistical technique popularized by Vermeesch (2013). The MDS method is a ‘superset of principal component analysis’ that, given a table of pairwise ‘dissimilarities’ between samples, produces a ‘map’ of points on which ‘similar’ samples cluster closely together and ‘dissimilar’ samples plot far apart (Vermeesch, 2013). Following the latest recommendations by Vermeesch (2018), we used the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to produce an MDS map comparing the analysed samples. The closest and second closest neighbours are linked by solid and dashed lines, respectively, and the goodness of fit was evaluated using the ‘stress’ value of the configuration (0.2 = poor; 0.1 = fair; 0.05 = good; Vermeesch, 2013). The MDS map was generated using the provenance package of Vermeesch et al. (2016). We also reported the maximum depositional age for one sample (MD61) calculating the ‘maximum likelihood age’ (MLA). The MLA is a statistical model that assumes that the zircon U–Pb ages defined a two component mixture, in which a ‘fraction of the population is derived from a discrete minimum age peak and the remaining grains follow a (log)normal distribution’ (see Vermeesch, 2021 and the references therein). The MLA was calculated using IsoplotR (Vermeesch, 2018).

## 4. Results

4.a. Stratigraphic constraints

Sample MD 189 (Figures 2 and 3, Table S3) was dated based on its palynological content (see the supplementary dataset for details). The presence of Retitriporites crotonicolumellatus from 18.4–0, Cichoreacidites longispinosus from 17.5–0, Polypodiaceoisporites pseudopsilatus from 16.9–0 Ma (Jaramillo et al. 2025) and Spirosyncolpites spiralis from 18.4–1.5 Ma (Jaramillo et al. 2025) all suggest that sample MD 189 is Early Miocene to Pleistocene in age. 4.c. U–Pb dating results

The U–Pb zircon age distributions of analysed samples of the Salvaci´on syncline and modern sands of the Madre de Dios River as well as the percentages of U–Pb zircon ages representing orogenic events of the Amazon craton and Andes are shown in Figures 8 and 9 and in Table 2, respectively. Details of the individual U–Pb zircon ages for each sample are presented in the supplementary material (Table S2) and in the supplementary information. The U–Pb age distributions of all analysed samples are dominated by zircon ages 0.9–1.3 Ga (Grenville/Sunsas), 0.5–0.7 Ga (Brasilian/Pampean), 290–252 Ma (Permian magmatism) and to a lesser extent by zircons ages younger than 130 Ma (Andean Arc) (Table 2 and Figures 8 and 9). The MLA age of MD 61 sample yields an age of 16.31 ± 0.28 Ma (Supplementary Fig. S3), which is in agreement with the “Pinturan” age (between 18.75 and 16.5 Ma) proposed by Marivaux et al. (2012). In the MDS graph (Figure 10), the Early to Middle Miocene samples (MD 61 and MD 252) and the modern Madre de Dios River sediments are connected by solid lines suggesting that they have quite similar U–Pb zircon age distributions. The Middle Miocene samples (MD 243 and MD 61) are also connected by solid and dashed lines with the Permian Mitu

sandstones analysed in Spikings et al. (2016). The Late Miocene (MD 246) sample is connected by solid lines with the Palaeocene samples analysed in Louterbach et al. (2018b) suggesting a good degree of similarity. The Pleistocene sample (MD 251) is connected by dashed lines to the Paleozoic metasediments of the EC analysed in Reimann et al. (2010) and Bahlburg et al. (2011). The Maastrichtian samples analysed in Louterbach et al. (2018b) plot apart from the analysed samples, suggesting that they are dissimilar. Hence, based on Table 2 and Figures 8, 9 and 10, two main differences in U–Pb zircon age distributions can be found along the stratigraphic succession, indicating two main changes in zircon distributions along the succession. The Early to Middle Miocene samples are characterized by an important contribution of Palaeozoic magmatic (especially Permian) zircons. This Permian contribution is dominant for the Middle Miocene sample MD 243 (55.1%, Table 2). The first change was observed between the Middle and Late Miocene. The Late Miocene sample MD 246 is characterized by an increase of Cretaceous Andean Arc and Grenville/Sunsas zircon (13.9% and 56.3%, respectively) and a strong decrease in the Palaeozoic magmatic zircon contribution (3.8%) compared with the Early to Middle Miocene samples. The second change is seen between the Pleistocene and the Late Miocene. The youngest Pleistocene sample (MD 251) has fewer contributions of Cretaceous Andean Arc (1.2%) and Grenville/ Sunsas (31.8%) zircons, but a higher contribution of Brazilian/ Pampean and Rondonia-San Ignacio zircons (20.0% and 15.3%, respectively) than the late Miocene sample (MD 246). When compared with the Neogene sandstones of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (Moizinho et al. 2023), most of the analysed samples plot apart from the ‘Neogene Inambari’ field and show no connection with these samples, with the exception of the Pleistocene sample (MD 251) and to a lesser extent, the Early Miocene MD 252 sample.

## 5. Discussion

5.a. Provenance interpretation

Sedimentary sorting, weathering and diagenesis might influence the concentrations of major and trace elements and prevent the use of Eu anomalies, Cr/Th ratios and Th/Sc ratios, for determining the provenance of sedimentary rock (McLennan et al. 1993). The effect of sedimentary sorting may be evaluated using the Al/Si ratio which is a proxy of grain size (Bouchez et al. 2011). In this study, the absence of any particular correlation between the Al/Si ratio and Eu/Eu*, Cr/Th and ƐNd (Supplementary Table S6) suggests that sedimentary sorting has not modified these provenance proxies. Additionally, the absence of negative Ce anomalies (ΩCe, Table S4) excludes the presence of significant authigenic smectite

that could have possibly formed during post-depositional diagenetic processes (Rodrigues et al. 2023). To summarize, we are confident that the Eu anomaly, Cr/Th and Th/Sc ratios, as well as Nd isotopic compositions, of analysed samples can be used here as robust provenance proxies. The Eu anomalies, the Cr/Th ratios and the Th/Sc ratios support a silicic/felsic nature for source rocks. Indeed, fine-grained sedimentary rocks derived from silicic/felsic sources are characterized by low Eu/Eu* ratios (0.3–0.94), high Th/ Sc (> 0.64) and low Cr/Th (< 15) (Cullers, 2000). Additionally, the provenance of Amazonian sedimentary rocks can be distinguished using their Nd isotopic composition (Basu et al. 1990; Roddaz et al. 2005). Sedimentary rocks sourced from the Cratonic regions of the Amazon Basin are characterized by more negative ƐNd(0) values, between −13.8 and −25, compared to Andean-derived sediments (Roddaz et al. 2005; Figueiredo et al. 2009; Nie et al. 2012; Horbe et al. 2013; Hoorn et al. 2017; Rodrigues et al. 2023). The ƐNd(0) values of the analysed samples are higher than −9.8, hence suggesting an Andean source for the Neogene sediments of the Salvaci´on syncline. Modern Sr–Nd isotopic compositions of suspended particulate matter (SPM) transported by tropical south American rivers have different isotopic compositions depending on their drainage basin (Allègre et al. 1996; Viers et al. 2008; Santos et al. 2015; Rousseau et al. 2019), and can be used for reconstructing past drainage configuration in the Amazon Basin. In the 87Sr/86Sr vs ƐNd(0) diagram (Figure 11), the analysed Neogene samples from the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin plot close to the Altiplano and Solimões SPM fields indicating a similar Andean source and a lithologically similar drainage basin to that of the Solimões. In this diagram (Figure 11), the analysed samples can be distinguished from the Neogene samples of the northern Bolivian SAZ (Roddaz et al. 2005) and the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (Moizinho et al. 2023), which plot closer to the SAZ and Madeira SPM fields. These findings suggest that the Neogene fine-grained sedimentary rocks of the northern part of the Madre de Dios basin have a different Andean source than those of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin. The REE composition of leached Fe-oxide fractions from sediments in the Madre de Dios Basin further reveals provenance differences between its northern and southern sectors. Recent studies have shown that mid-REE (MREE) enrichment in Feoxides – expressed using the concavity index (CI = GdN/(La6N × Yb7N)1/13; Bayon et al. 2020) – is a sensitive tracer of lithological contrasts in drainage basins. In the northern Pongo de Co˜neq area (see Figures 2 and 3 for location), Fe-oxides exhibit markedly elevated CI values (4.1 ± 2.6, n = 4; Fig. 7a). In contrast, samples from the southern Inambari region (see Figures 2 and 3 for location) show much lower CI values (1.3 ± 0.4, n = 6; Figure 7b). High CI values (>2.5) are characteristic of regions where oxidative weathering of sulfide-bearing rocks – particularly black shales – can drive the formation of secondary Fe-oxides under low-pH conditions. In these regions, black shale weathering is accompanied by preferential dissolution of MREE-enriched phosphate minerals such as apatite, which can release substantial amounts of dissolved REE in soils than can be subsequently incorporated into neoformed Fe-oxides in soils (Bayon et al. 2020; Jang et al. 2024; Moizinho et al. 2026). In this study, it is noteworthy that the Upper Madeira region, where the Pongo de Co˜neq samples were collected, is widely recognized as a hotspot for sulfide oxidation in the Amazon headwaters (Moquet et al. 2011, 2016; Torres et al. 2015, 2016; Dellinger et al. 2023). In contrast, the Inambari samples lack significant MREE enrichment, suggesting limited influence from sulfide weathering

Finally, a difference in provenance between the Neogene sedimentary rocks of the northern and southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin can be also inferred from the U–Pb zircon age distributions. The U–Pb zircon age distribution of the northern part of the Madre de Dios is characterized by the presence of Cretaceous to Cenozoic Andean arc zircons, whereas these zircons are absent from the Neogene samples from the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin (Moizinho et al. 2023). The difference in provenance is also confirmed by the statistical analysis of the U–Pb zircon distributions of the Neogene samples as shown in the MDS maps (Figure 10 and Supplementary Figs S4 and S5). In these maps, the Neogene sedimentary rocks of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin, which were interpreted to be sourced by the EC and SAZ (Moizinho et al. 2023) define a distinct group when compared with the sedimentary rocks from the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin. Regarding sediment provenance, all studied samples display a significant proportion of zircons younger than 500 Ma, which typifies an Andean provenance (Hurtado et al. 2018; Chavez et al. 2022; Table 3). The presence of Cretaceous and Cenozoic zircons further suggests a subordinate contribution from the Altiplano in all of the samples (Tables 2 and 3) It should be noted that a dominant and significant proportion of Grenville/Sunsas U–Pb zircon ages (0.9–1.3 Ga) in all analysed samples are not useful for differentiating Andean and cratonic sources because the Grenville/Sunsas zircons can be found elsewhere in the Andes (Coastal Cordillera, Altiplano, and EC, Table 3) or in the Amazon craton (Table 3). In addition, the MDS map shows different contributions of the source area during the Neogene. The Early to Middle Miocene sample (MD 252) plots close to the modern sands of the Madre de Dios River, sampled at Puerto Maldonado (MDD River), indicating similar contribution from the different

Andean sources. The Middle Miocene samples (MD 243 and MD 61) are connected with the Permian Mitu sandstones analysed in Spikings et al. (2016) by solid and dashed lines, indicating a similar provenance. We interpret a dominant EC source because the plutonic Permo-Triassic rocks and the volcanic rocks of the Mitu Formation are in the EC (Spikings et al. 2016). In addition, we suggest that the strong increase in Permian zircon contributions, the decrease in Brazilian/Pampean zircon contribution and the absence of Cenozoic Andean Arc zircons in the MD 243 sample may be the result of the increasing erosion of the EC. The Late Miocene (MD 246) and Pleistocene (MD 251) samples plot apart from the Middle Miocene samples. The Late Miocene sample (MD 246) is connected to the Paleocene samples of the Pongo de Co˜neq area analysed in Louterbach et al. (2018), suggesting a similar provenance. The Pleistocene sample (MD 251) is connected with solid line with the Plio-Pleistocene sample of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin by a solid line, suggesting a shared provenance. This sample is also connected to the Palaeozoic metasediments of the Eastern Cordillera analysed in Reimann et al. (2010) and Bahlburg et al. (2011) by dashed line. We suggest that this Pleistocene sample has greater contributions from the recycled sedimentary rocks of the SAZ, indicating increasing erosion and deformation of the SAZ. This latter hypothesis is supported by (i) the high content of reworked Palaeozoic megaspores found in sample MD 189 which is stratigraphically between MD 246 and MD 251 (Figure 5), (ii) by the increasing contribution of the Brazilian/Pampean zircons to the Pleistocene sample (MD 251) and (iii) by the presence of welldeveloped Pleistocene growth strata deposits in the Salvaci´on synline that suggest Pleistocene growth of the Pantiacolla anticline and Pongo de Coneq structures (Louterbach, 2014; Baby et al. 2018a; Figures 2 and 3 for location).

5.b. Paleogeography and biological implications

Our provenance investigation indicates that two different drainage basins with different Andean sources coexisted during the Neogene in the Madre de Dios Basin (Figures 12 and 13). The northern part of the Basin is characterized by Solimoes-like ƐNd(0) values for fined grained sedimentary rocks, authigenic Fe-oxides formed from sulfide oxidation processes and zircons sourced from the Altiplano, EC and SAZ. In contrast, the southern part displays fine grained sedimentary rocks with Madeira-like ƐNd(0) composition, Fe-oxides formed via silicate weathering processes and zircon derived from the EC and SAZ (Moizinho et al. 2023). Several mechanisms/processes may account for the coexistence of two drainage basins in the same retroarc foreland basin system during the Neogene.

Autocyclic change in sedimentary patterns such as stream avulsion or point bar migration which are produced by processes within the sedimentary system (Cecil, 2003) might induce local change in sedimentary provenance. However we found this hypothesis unlikely because (i) both depositional sequences 1 and 2 from the Pongo Coneq area and the first sequence of the Inambari area consist of meandering or fluvial channel developed in an extensive floodplain area (Louterbach, 2014; Moizinho et al. 2023) and show no provenance variation upsection (Moizinho et al. 2023; this study) and (ii) the youngest depositional sequences of both area which consists of braided river or alluvial fan deposits show no provenance variation upsections. Differential erosion, linked to marked changes in the spatial distribution of precipitation (rainfall) in the source area, could possibly account for the difference in

provenance between the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin during the Neogene. However, we find this hypothesis unlikely because there is no evidence of for such differences in rainfall or climatic regimes between the two studied areas during the Neogene. Instead, previous studies have suggested that the Madre de Dios Basin experienced a similar climatic regime to the northern Bolivian Beni Basin (McQuarrie et al. 2008) and that the EC adjacent to both basins was affected by a widespread Pliocene incision probably due to the combined effects of changes in paleoclimate (Lease and Ehlers, 2013; Falkowski et al. 2023) and tectonic surface uplift and deformation in both the EC and SAZ (Moizinho et al. 2023). Differences in the surface uplift of the EC and Altiplano due to differences in deformation might also explain the difference in provenance found between the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin. We also found this hypothesis to be unlikely because no significant difference in the Neogene deformation of the SAZ was found to the south to latitude 12°S (Mora et al. 2011; Baby et al. 2018a, b). The available palaeoelevation model also suggests no difference in surface uplift between the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin (Sundell et al. 2019). Also, it was not possible to correlate the seismic reflectors identified in the Pongo de Coneq area with those identified in the Inambari area (Louterbach, 2014). A possible explanation for the impossibility of seismic and fault correlations could be the presence of unmapped transfer fault or other structures located between the two area, somewhere between 71°00 and 70°30W longitude (Figures 2 and 3). In fold and trust belt, transfer faults can develop due to reactivation of pre-existing strike slip and/or normal faults. The presence of such transfer fault has been documented elsewhere in fold and thrust belt around the world including in the Andes and Pyrenees (e.g. Espurt et al. 2008; Mu˜noz, 2017). However, with the dataset we have, more geomorphological and structural works in the Madre de Dios fold and thrust belt are needed to identify correctly the presence of these transfer faults. Interestingly, different provenance was found for the Cretaceous sedimentary rocks from the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin (Rodrigues et al. 2023). Maastrichtian sedimentary rocks from the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin were sourced by the central part of the Amazonian craton and were part of the same palaeo-drainage system as those located in the other Peruvian and Ecuadorian Amazonian basins (Rodrigues et al. 2023). In contrast, coeval Cretaceous rocks of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin were sourced by local cratonic sources and were not connected with this craton wide palaeo-drainage system. Although Palaeogene provenance data are lacking for the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin, we speculate that the drainage divide highlighted in our study might be inherited from Cretaceous times. Given the fact that the sedimentary rocks of the northern part of Madre de Dios Basin have Solimoes-like ƐNd(0) values and those of the southern part have Madeira-like ƐNd(0) values, we propose that the southern limit of the Maastrichtian to Mio-Pliocene Amazonian palaeo-drainage basin was located within the Madre de Dios Basin (Figure 13). Finally, it follows that the uplift of the Fitzcarrald Arch during the Pliocene (Espurt et al. 2007, 2011a) is responsible for the latest reorganization of the Amazonian drainage and hence is the mechanism at the origin of the modern configuration of the Amazonian drainage (Figures 12 and 13). A major implication of our findings is that the presence of a long-lived Cretaceous to Pliocene drainage divide between the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin might have promoted endemism and species diversification at that time. Major rivers and their drainage dynamics are suspected to significantly affect the allopatric speciation of Amazonian vertebrates in the Plio-Pleistocene (Ribas et al. 2011). Recent studies have also highlighted the role of landscape dynamics in shaping the geological history of drainage basin connections on the assembly and diversification of Amazonian ‘basin-wide fish faunas’ since the Palaeogene (Cassemiro et al. 2023). For example, Musher et al. (2022) ascribed the Cenozoic diversification of the Tityridae (bird) families in the Amazon Basin to be partly caused by barrier displacement and a dynamic spatially heterogenous landscape. Similarly, tectonically driven Amazonian river captures such as the transcontinentalization of the Amazon River that connected eastern and western Amazonia or the Pliocene Fitzcarrald Arch uplift (Espurt et al. 2007, 2011a) during the Neogene are suspected to have played a major role in the lineage diversification of taxa in the lowlands of the Amazon Basin (Albert et al. 2021, and the references therein). The region of the Fitzcarrald Arch, including the Madre de Dios Basin, has high fish diversity, including relatively ancient fish species that originated before the uplift of the

Fitzcarrald Arch (Albert et al. 2011). The richness of fish species in the Amazon Basin is higher in the western part with fish dispersal progressing eastward (Oberdorff et al. 2019) after the Amazon River became transcontinental during the Late Miocene (Figueiredo et al. 2009; Gorini et al. 2014; van Soelen et al. 2017) and the Pliocene uplift of the Fitzcarrald Arch (Espurt et al. 2007, 2011a). Interestingly, the Madre de Dios Basin has one of the highest fish species diversity and endemic richness of western Amazonian basins (Oberdorff et al. 2019). This characteristic probably originated from Miocene times and may be due to its geographic isolation (dispersal limitation). We therefore suggest that the long-lived drainage divide within the Madre de Dios Basin might be one of the drivers for the inherited high diversity and rich endemism of the fish species.

## 6. Conclusions

The combination of field work, stratigraphic correlation (using a new subsurface dataset) and provenance data (major and trace element concentrations, REE of Fe-oxides, Sr–Nd isotopes and zircon U–Pb dating) from the Madre de Dios Basin yields the following conclusions:

• The fine-grained Neogene sedimentary rocks of the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin have trace element ratios (Cr/ Th and Th/Sc) and REE patterns that typify a felsic/silicic source; • They are characterized by Solimões-like ƐNd(0) values for fine-grained sedimentary rocks and zircons sourced from the Altiplano and EC; • Contrasting REE composition of leached Fe-oxides in the Pongo de Coneq and Inambari sections indicates different lithological sources between the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin; • The zircon age distribution of the Neogene sedimentary rocks indicates sources located in the Altiplano, EC and SAZ; • The Neogene sedimentary rocks of the northern part of the Madre de Dios Basin have a different provenance than the Neogene sedimentary rocks of the southern part of the Madre de Dios Basin, which are characterized by Madeira-like ƐNd(0) values and zircon sourced from the EC and SAZ (Moizinho et al. 2023); • The observed difference in provenance likely reflects the existence of a palaeogeographic barrier within the Madre de Dios retroarc foreland Basin, although its exact location and the mechanisms responsible for its presence during the Neogene remain unclear.

Finally, given that the Cretaceous sedimentary rocks of the northern and southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin have different provenance (Rodrigues et al. 2023), we propose that the southern limit of the Maastrichtian to Plio-Pleistocene Amazonian palaeo-drainage basin was located within the Madre de Dios Basin. We also speculate that this long-lived intrabasinal drainage divide might be a driver for endemism and species diversification within the Madre de Dios Basin.

Abstract 19

The geological history of the Amazon River is a complex story driven by geodynamic 20

processes operating in the South American plate. In spite of recent research, the pre- 21

Neogene structure of Amazon paleodrainage is still underconstrained. A recent study 22

has suggested that the western Amazonian paleodrainage system was reversed, 23

cratonic in origin during the Cretaceous. However, the extent and duration of this 24

system are not well-constrained. To add new constraints, we investigated the 25

sources of Cretaceous sedimentary rocks in the Brazilian Acre and Peruvian Madre 26

de Dios basins, based on major and trace element concentrations, Sm-Nd isotopic 27

compositions, and U-Pb detrital zircon dating. The late Cretaceous samples of the 28

Acre Basin have ƐNd (0) values between -21.2 and -8.4 and zircon grains derived 29

from terranes situated in the easternmost part of the Amazonian Craton: Ventuari- 30

Tapajos (2.0-1.82 Ga) and Rio Negro -Juruena (1.82-1.54 Ga). In contrast, the 31

Madre de Dios Basin samples have εNd (0) values ranging from -15.2 to -7.1 and a 32

wide range of U-Pb zircon age distributions. The samples from the northern part of 33

the basin (MD234 and MD238) are dominated by zircon ages between 0.9-1.3 Ga 34

(Grenville/ Sunsás, 30% - 43%) and 0.5-0.7 Ga (Brazilian/Pampean, 26% - 16%) with 35

felsic provenance. The oldest MD234 sample also shows a dominant contribution 36

from Paleozoic zircon (20%). On the other hand, the samples from the southern part 37

of the Madre de Dios Basin (samples MD-2019-4A; MD-2019-10; MD-2019-13; MD- 38

2019-11D and MD-2019-12A) have U-Pb age distributions dominated by zircon ages 39

between 0.9-1.3 Ga (Grenville/Sunsás, 30% - 45%) and 1.54-1.3 Ga (Rondonia-San 40

Ignácio, 16% - 43%), pointing to a cratonic origin for these sedimentary rocks. To 41

elucidate the distinction in provenance between the samples from the northern and 42

southern parts of the Madre de Dios Basin, we suggest that a structural barrier (the 43

Madidi Arch (?)) was active during the late Cretaceous. In this scenario, the northern 44

part of the Madre de Dios Basin had similar sedimentary sources as the nearby 45

basins like Huallaga, Bagua, Ucayali, and Marañón, whereas, in the southern part of 46

the basin, sedimentation was influenced by local sources. Together with previously 47


<!-- Page 4 -->


published studies, these data indicate that the continent-wide cratonic drainage 48

developed between the Cenomanian and Maastrichtian in response to the Purus 49

Arch uplift was probably driven by a geodynamic process related to the post-rift 50

opening of the Atlantic Equatorial Ocean. 51

1. Introduction 54

In terms of global mass transfer from continents to oceans, the Amazon River 55

is the most important river contributor, supplying about 20% of the water (Callède et 56

al., 2004), ~10% of the dissolved load (Gaillardet et al., 2003), and ~3% of the 57

suspended load (Milliman & Syvitski, 1992) to the world’s oceans. According to 58

Filizola & Guyot, (2004), Andean tributaries supply more than 95% of the median 59

annual suspended sediment flux that the Amazon delivers, with 2/3 and 1/3 from the 60

Solimões and Madeira rivers, respectively. Its basin drainage includes several Meso- 61

Cenozoic basins located between the Andes and the Atlantic Ocean (Fig. 1). The 62

geological history of the Amazon River and its paleodrainage is complex and its 63

Neogene configuration is a much-discussed subject (Albert et al., 2018; Hoorn et al., 64

2010; Carina Hoorn et al., 2017; Louterbach et al., 2018; Roddaz et al., 2005, 2010; 65

van Soelen et al., 2017a). The majority of previous research has concentrated on two 66

aspects concerning the Amazon River: the precise moment of its 67

transcontinentalization (Figueiredo et al., 2009; Gorini et al., 2014; Hoorn et al., 2017; 68

van Soelen et al., 2017b) and the  geodynamic systems, such as Andean uplift, flat- 69

slab subduction or dynamic topography, that potentially drove this (Eakin et al., 2014; 70

Rodríguez Tribaldos et al., 2017; Sacek, 2014; Shephard et al., 2010). In spite of 71


<!-- Page 5 -->


new researches (e.g. Hurtado et al., 2018; Rodríguez Tribaldos et al., 2017; Stewart 72

et al., 2016), the Amazon basin’s pre-Neogene arrangement has garnered 73

considerably less focus. 74

Recent studies on sedimentary rocks from the Peruvian and Ecuadorian retro 75

arc foreland basins have shown major changes in the drainage system of the 76

western Amazon between the Albian and the early Paleocene (Erlich et al., 2018; 77

George et al., 2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Hurtado et al., 2018; et al., 2018). Based 78

on the ɛNd values (between – 16.8 to -18.6) and the detrital zircon grain, which were 79

originated from the easternmost Brazilian Shield terranes Hurtado et al. (2018) 80

suggested the existence of a long-lived cratonic drainage system originated from the 81

Purus Arch (Fig. 1) in the Central-Eastern part of the Brazilian Shield during the 82

Albian-Maastrichtian (from ca 110 Ma to 66 Ma). This cratonic drainage system may 83

be considered the western part of the Cretaceous continent-wide cratonic drainage of 84

the northern part of South America termed “Sanozama” paleodrainage (Almeida, 85

1974; Potter, 1997). However, the study of Hurtado et al. (2018) is based on two 86

Cretaceous samples from the Huallaga Basin and one from the northern part of the 87

Madre de Dios Basin. Hence, the extent and duration of this continent-wide cratonic 88

drainage system during the Cretaceous and how it detected other western 89

Amazonian basins is far from being constrained. 90

In this study, we refine the extent and duration of the long-lived cratonic 91

drainage system in Western Amazonia based on the provenance study of 92

Cretaceous sedimentary rocks deposited in the Acre and Madre de Dios basins. We 93

present whole-rock geochemistry, Sm-Nd isotopic composition, and U-Pb zircon 94

ages to understand the regional configuration and evolution of western Amazonian 95

basins. Through compilations with recent studies, our data indicate that the long-lived 96


<!-- Page 6 -->


paleodrainage system developed between the Cenomanian and Maastrichtian and 97

reached its maximum paleogeographic extension in the Maastrichtian in response to 98

the Purus Arch uplift. 99

2. Geological settings and sampling 101

2.1. Cretaceous stratigraphy of western Amazonian basins 102

The Cretaceous paleogeography of northern South America was strongly 103

controlled by the geodynamic process related to Gondwana’s breakup and the 104

convergence between the Nazca and South America plates (Zamora & Gil, 2018). 105

Since Cretaceous times western Amazonia (Fig.1) sedimentary basins, such as the 106

Oriente/Marañón, Santiago, Bagua, Ucayali, Huallaga, Madre de Dios, and Acre 107

basins experienced a complex structural evolution (Baby et al., 2005; Erlich et al., 108

2018; George et al., 2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Hermoza et al., 2006; Louterbach et 109

al., 2018; Martinez et al., 1999; Roddaz et al., 2005; Wine et al., 2001; Zamora & Gil, 110

2018) (Figs. 1 and 2). These basins are presently divided into two parts, the northern 111

and the southern Amazonian retroarc foreland basin (N. Espurt et al., 2007; Roddaz 112

et al., 2005b), because of the uplift of the Fitzcarrald Arch in the Pliocene (Espurt et 113

al., 2007); ( Espurt et al., 2010; Roddaz et al., 2010). 114

The Oriente Basin is made up of Paleozoic to Quaternary sedimentary rocks 115

and sediments (Christophoul et al., 2002). Prolonged to the north by the Putumayo 116

Basin of Colombia and to the south by the Marañón Basin (Fig. 1), the Oriente Basin 117

displays three stratigraphic units ranging in age from the Carboniferous to the Recent 118

(Baby et al., 1999). The first Cretaceous sequence is formed by the Hollin and Napo 119

Formations, which is composed of sandstones, limestones, and organic-rich shales 120

(Fig. 2). The Albian sandstones from the Hollin Formation were deposited above the 121


<!-- Page 7 -->


pre-Albian unconformity (Baby et al., 2013) and derived from the Amazon craton 122

(Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Ruiz et al., 2007). The Upper Cretaceous Napo Formation 123

sedimentary rocks are derived from eastern cratonic sources, mainly from the 124

Rondonian-San Ignacio terrane (1.8 – 1.3 Ga) (Gutiérrez et al., 2019). The Tena 125

Formation (Maastrichtian-Paleocene) exhibits fine-grained reddish sediments that 126

were deposited in a fluvial setting within a distal foredeep deposition zone (Baby et 127

al., 2013). The sedimentary sources were related to the exhumation of the Cordillera 128

Real to the west (Ruiz et al., 2004) and the recycling of ancient formations (Hollin 129

and Napo formations) (Gutiérrez et al., 2019). 130

The Cretaceous sequences of the Oriente Basin are correlated to those of the 131

Marañón Basin (Zamora & Gil, 2018), which is located southward between the 132

Ucayali and Acre basins (Fig. 1). The Cretaceous sedimentary succession within the 133

Marañón Basin begins with the deposition of the sandstones of the Cushabatay 134

Formation in a fluvial to shoreface environments as a product from the Jurua orogeny 135

reactivation (Caputo, 2014; Zamora & Gil, 2018). The Cretaceous sedimentary rocks 136

were deposited after an erosional hiatus (110-120 Ma) and are the calcareous green 137

shales, interbedded with sandstones and platform limestones of the Raya Formation 138

(equivalent to the Napo Basal in the Oriente Basin; Fig. 2) (Zamora and Gil, 2018). 139

The Albian to early Cenomanian Agua Caliente Formation is characterized by 140

sandstones and shales deposited into fluvial-deltaic and marine settings (Zamora & 141

Gil, 2018) The transition between this formation and the Chonta Formation is 142

progressive (Wine et al., 2001; Zamora & Gil, 2018). The Chonta Formation is 143

composed of sandstones, limestones, and shales and consists of the source rock of 144

the Oriente - Marañón prolific oil province (Calderon et al., 2017). This unit defines 145

three transgressive-regressive sequences (Zamora and Gil, 2018). During the 146


<!-- Page 8 -->


Turonian, limestones and black shales were deposited. From the Coniacian to 147

Santonian marine shales interbedded with sandstones and limestones were 148

deposited. The contact between the Chonta Formation and the middle Campanian - 149

late Maastrichtian, fluvial to shallow marine Vivian Formation is erosive (Calderon et 150

al., 2017; Zamora & Gil, 2018). The late Maastrichtian Vivian-Cachiyacu formations 151

represent the last Cretaceous deposition cycle and were formed by sandstones, 152

shales, and limestones (Calderon et al., 2017) (Fig. 2). 153

The Ucayali Basin is limited from the Marañón Basin by the NW-SE Contaya 154

Arch and from the Acre Basin, by the NNW-SSE Moa Divisor structure (Fig. 1). The 155

sedimentary thickness of the basin decreases progressively to the south and towards 156

the Fitzcarrald Arch (Hermoza et al., 2006; Lopez-Gamundi & Lopez-Gamundi, 157

2018). The Cretaceous sedimentation started with the Cushabatay and Raya 158

formations during the Neocomian – Aptian (Martinez et al., 1999). They consist of 159

fluvial to marginal clastics and marine limestones, which progressively disappear to 160

the NNE/SSW (Fig. 2) (Martinez et al., 1999). The Chonta Formation is made up of 161

shales and limestones (Calderon et al., 2017). The end of the Cretaceous is 162

represented by the Maastrichtian quartz-rich sandstones of the Vivian Formation 163

(Martinez et al., 1999). 164

The Huallaga Basin is bounded by the Eastern Cordillera to the west and the 165

Chazuta thrust-related anticline to the east (Hurtado et al., 2018). An erosional 166

unconformity separates the Cretaceous sedimentary succession which is made up 167

from the bottom to the top, by the Cushabatay, Raya, Agua Caliente, Chonta, 168

Cashiyacu, and Vivian formations. The Cushabatay Formation consists of quartz-rich 169

sandstones interbedded with shales and siltstones and deposited by fluvial-deltaic 170

systems during Aptian-Albian times (Hurtado et al., 2018; Wine et al., 2001). The 171


<!-- Page 9 -->


middle-late Albian Raya Formation was deposited in a shallow marine environment 172

and consists of shales, siltstones, and sparse calcareous beds (Hurtado et al., 2018; 173

Sanchez et al., 1997). The Cenomanian Agua Caliente deposits are composed of 174

fluvial-deltaic sandstones interbedded with shales and siltstones (Sanchez et al., 175

1997). The Coniacian-Turonian Chonta Formation is composed of marine shales, 176

marls, mudstones, and limestones (Hurtado et al., 2018). This stratigraphic pile ends 177

in the Maastrichtian with the fluvial coastal quartz-rich sandstones of the Vivian 178

Formation whose marine equivalent is the Cachiyacu Formation (Hurtado et al., 179

2018; Sanchez et al., 1997). 180

The southern Peruvian Madre de Dios Basin is limited to the southwest by the 181

Azulmayo thrust, to the north and northeast by the Brazilian Shield, and to the north- 182

northwest by the Fitzcarrald Arch ( Louterbach et al., 2018). The basement of the 183

basin includes Precambrian to Cambrian metamorphic rocks, Paleozoic 184

metasediments, and tardi-Hercynian igneous rocks ( Louterbach et al., 2018). To the 185

east at the boundary with the Eastern Cordillera, the Madre de Dios Basin 186

encompasses a heterogeneous sedimentary succession of sedimentary rocks 187

deposited between the Upper Paleozoic and the Cenozoic ( Louterbach et al., 2018). 188

The deposits from the early Cretaceous did not undergo preservation, while the 189

sedimentary succession of the late Cretaceous began above a basal regional 190

unconformity (Louterbach, 2014). It is then followed by estuarine sandstones from 191

the Basal Chonta Formation followed by littoral to intertidal gray carbonaceous 192

shales, mudstones siltstones, and sandstones from the Cenomanian-Turonian 193

Chonta Formation (Louterbach, 2014). The Vivian Formation started with red shales 194

and paleosol horizons formed during the late Campanian in a fluvial-tidal coastal 195

plain (Louterbach et al., 2018). The late Maastrichtian Vivian Formation is 196


<!-- Page 10 -->


characterized by sandstones, deposited in a coastal environment with continental 197

inputs (Louterbach, 2014; Louterbach et al., 2018). 198

The Acre Basin is limited to the east and north by the Iquitos Arch, to the 199

northwest by the Marañón Basin, to the west by the Ucayali Basin, and to the south 200

by the Madre de Dios Basin (Cunha, 2007; Haag, 2019). According to (Oliveira, 201

1994), this basin was affected by complex compressional and extensional events 202

from the Paleozoic to the Present. The Albian-Cenomanian sandstones from the 203

lower Moa Formation were followed by transgressive Cenomanian/Turonian black 204

shales of the upper part of this unit. During the Turonian-Campanian, black shales 205

and fine-grained sandstones of the Rio Azul Formation were deposited. The late 206

Campanian Divisor Formation was made up of fluvial sandstones (Cunha, 2007). 207

The sedimentary units from the late Cretaceous of the Marañón, Ucayali, 208

Huallaga, Madre de Dios, and Acre basins may be correlated with the Alter do Chão 209

Formation from the Solimões and Amazonia basins (Caputo, 2014; Hurtado et al., 210

2018). The Jurassic Envira Arch separates the Acre from the Solimões Basin and the 211

Purus Arch limited the Solimões and Amazonas basins (Caputo, 2014) (Fig. 1). The 212

Purus Arch formed as a result of Neoproterozoic compressive stress that caused the 213

inversion of the Cachimbo Graben (Caputo & Soares, 2016; Wanderley Filho et al., 214

2007). The Purus Arch experienced episodes of uplift and subsidence after the 215

Pennsylvanian (Caputo & Soares, 2016; Wanderley Filho et al., 2007). Because of 216

the presence of the Cenozoic deposits and the absence of the Cretaceous 217

sedimentary rocks around the Purus Arch (Caputo & Soares, 2016), the Purus Arch 218

could be topographically high during the Cretaceous as Hurtado et al. (2018) 219

suggested. 220

2.2. Potential sources 222

Detrital zircon U-Pb ages have been used in provenance studies in the Andes- 223

Amazonian basins to interpret the possible contributions of Cratonic and Andean 224

source rocks during the sedimentary evolution (Chavez et al., 2022; Erlich et al., 225

2018; George et al., 2019; Horton et al., 2015; Horton, 2018; Hurtado et al., 2018; 226

Louterbach et al., 2018; Moreno et al., 2020; Nie et al., 2012). The relative sources 227

have different types of terranes and different ages. Precambrian zircon U-Pb ages 228

(>900 Ma) are found in the Amazon craton which is a continental block resulting from 229

lateral crustal accretionary processes that lasted from Archean to Mesoproterozoic 230

(Cordani & Teixeira, 2007; Santos et al., 2000; Tassinari & Macambira, 1999). 231

Neoproterozoic and Phanerozoic zircon U-Pb ages (<900 Ma) could be related to 232

rocks from the fold and thrust belts formed during the amalgamation of the 233

Supercontinent Gondwana. These rocks were affected by the Brazilian Event (Brito 234

Neves, 2002), and by magmatic events on western Gondwana related to a polycyclic 235

orogenic history ( Chew et al., 2008; Chew et al., 2007; Chew et al., 2016) (Fig. 3). 236

Nd isotopes may be used as a provenance tool because they are not easily 237

fractionated by sedimentary or post-depositional processes (Konieczna et al., 2015; 238

Mahoney, 2005; McLennan et al., 1990). Cratonic-derived river sediments have 239

εNd(0) values between -14.5 and -20, while Andean-derived sediments have εNd(0) 240

values >-13.8 (Figueiredo et al., 2009; Horbe et al., 2013; Roddaz et al., 2005). This 241

difference in the Nd isotopes recorded in fine-grained sediments has been used to 242

decipher the provenance and reconstruct the paleodrainage systems in Western 243

Amazonia (e. g. Roddaz et al., 2005; Louterbach et al., 2018; Hurtado et al., 2018). 244

2.3. Sampling and stratigraphic constraints 245


<!-- Page 12 -->


In total, we collected thirty-five samples from the Cretaceous sedimentary rock 246

successions cropping out in the Madre de Dios and Acre basins (Fig. 2 and details in 247

the supplementary dataset). Among these samples, seven from the Madre de Dios 248

Basin and seven from the Acre Basin were analyzed for zircon U-Pb dating. For 249

comparisons, we used data from two samples from Louterbach et al. (2018) (MD 239 250

and MD 176, Table 1). Eighteen samples were measured for their major and trace 251

elements concentrations (seven from the Madre de Dios Basin and eleven from the 252

Acre Basin). Twenty-two samples were measured for their whole-rock Sm-Nd 253

isotopic composition (eleven from Madre de Dios Basin and eleven from the Acre 254

Basin). The locations of the analyzed samples can be found in Table 1 and the 255

supplementary dataset. 256

3. Materials and methods 313

3.1. Major and trace element concentrations 314

The major and trace element concentrations were measured at the Service 315

d’Analyse des Roches et Mineraux (SARM, INSU facility, Vandoeuvre-Les-Nancy, 316

France) by ICP-OES and ICP-MS. Analytical details are available on 317

http://helium.crpg.cnrs-nancy.fr/SARM/ and in (Carignan et al., 2001). Precision is 318

better than 5% for elements measured by ICP-OES, and 10% for elements measured 319

by ICP-MS (see supplementary dataset for details). 320


<!-- Page 15 -->


3.2. Sm-Nd isotope composition 321

The Sm-Nd isotope composition of the analyzed was made at the Geochronos 322

Laboratory of the Geosciences Institute, Universidade de Brasília, following the 323

methods described by Goia & Pimentel (2000). The isotopic ratios of Sm and Nd 324

were measured using a Thermo Scientific TRITON Plus thermal ionization mass 325

spectrometer. The precision of the measurements was estimated by analyzing the 326

BHVO-2 standard and repeated analysis gave a 143Nd/144Nd ratio of 0.512996 ± 327

0.000006 (2SD, n=10) (Weis et al., 2005). 328

The measured 143Nd/144Ndsample and 143Sm/144Ndsample ratios were expressed in ɛ 329

notation and reflect the fractional deviation in parts per 104 unit from the 143Sm/144Nd 330

from the Chondritic Uniform Reservoir (CHUR) as described by Jacobsen & 331

Wasserburg (1980). The TDM and TDM* ages were calculated following (Augustsson 332

& Bahlburg, 2008; DePaolo et al., 1991; DePaolo, 1981; Albarède & Brouxel, 1987 333

and Goldstein et al., 1984) as demonstrated in the supplementary dataset. 334

3.3. Detrital zircon geochronological analysis 335

The samples were treated at the Geochronos Laboratory of the Geosciences 336

Institute, Universidade de Brasília. Approximately 150 zircon grains were handpicked 337

from each sample, mounted in epoxy resin, and polished to obtain a flat surface, 338

ideal for U-Pb analyses. Acquisition parameters, data reduction and reference 339

material information are summarized in Table S5 and S6 in the supplementary 340

dataset. 341

The 206Pb/238U ages were utilized for zircons grains with ages ≤1.5 Ga and 342

207Pb/206Pb ages for grains with ages >1.5 Ga (Spencer et al., 2016). Discordance 343

age degrees >10% were not considered, as well as samples with few zircons, 344

because of their low statistical representation (Vermeesch, 2004). The kernel density 345


<!-- Page 16 -->


estimation (KDE) diagrams (Vermeesch, 2013) were used to illustrate and compared 346

detrital zircon age data. To investigate the difference between detrital zircon U-Pb 347

age distributions, we employed the non-matrix metric multi-dimensional scaling 348

(MDS) statistical technique outlined by Vermeesch (2013). In accordance with the 349

latest recommendations  by Vermeesch (2018), we utilized the Kolmogorov–Smirnov 350

test to generate an MDS map that compares the analyzed samples. 351

4. Results 353

4.1. Major elements, Large-Ion Lithophile Elements (LILE), High Field Strength 354

Elements (HFSE), and Trace Transition Elements (TTE) 355

The elemental concentrations of major elements, LILE, HFSE, and TTE of 356

analyzed samples were normalized to the Post Archean Australian Shales (PAAS) 357

concentration (Pourmand et al., 2012; Taylor & McLennan, 1985) (Fig. 4). The 358

Chemical Index of Alteration (CIA) can be used to evaluate the level of the paleo- 359

weathering situation of ancient sediments and the weathering of the original area 360

(Fedo et al., 1995; Nesbitt & Young, 1982). The weathering intensity of feldspars in 361

comparation to unaltered rocks is quantified by the CIA= 362

[Al2O3/(Al2O3+CaO*+Na2)+K2O)] x 100 (in molar proportions), in which CaO* denotes 363

the concentration of CaO within silicate component. Because of the lack of CO2  data, 364

to calculate CaO*, we have assumed the value of CaO if Cao ≤ Na2O or CaO = Na2O 365

if CaO>Na2O (Bock et al., 1998). CIA values around 50 are commonly observed for 366

unaltered plagioclase and K-feldspars found in upper crustal rocks, while elevated 367

CIA values indicate increased levels of weathering. The CIA value of the PAAS 368

standard is 67 and represent the upper continental crust configuration (Taylor & 369

McLennan, 1985). The grain-size sorting effect can be valuated using the Al/Si ratio 370


<!-- Page 17 -->


as it can be considered a proxy for sediment grain size (Bouchez et al., 2011). The 371

sedimentary sorting effect favors heavy mineral concentrations such as zircon and 372

quartz dilution in the coarser fraction, which could modify the trace element ratios 373

used as provenance proxies (McLennan et al., 1993; Roddaz et al., 2014). 374

GdN)½ where N refers to the chondrite-normalized concentration value (Condie, 400

5. Discussion 477

5.1. Influence of geochemical characteristics in the provenance sedimentary 478

interpretation. 479

The utilization of elemental ratios (Cr/Th, Th/Sc, Zr/Sc), Eu anomalies 480

(Eu/Eu*) and Sm-Nd isotopic compositions of sedimentary rock have proven to be 481

valuable in determining the source of ancient sediments (McLennan et al., 1993). 482

However, it is essential to consider the potential effects of grain-size sorting and 483

diagenesis on trace element ratios, REE concentration, and radiogenic isotope 484

composition of the analyzed sedimentary rocks. 485

Except for the samples AC 33 (0.42) and AC 27A (0.44), most of the Acre 486

Basin samples have a low Al/Si ratio (0.01 - 0.27) (Fig. 6), which indicates that they 487

are enriched in quartz. However, the lack of Al/Si with REE content, Eu/Eu*, Cr/Th, 488

and ƐNd (0) correlation (seen in the supplementary dataset) suggests sedimentary 489

sorting has not made any alteration of these provenance indicators. Nevertheless, 490

the REE concentrations of the analyzed samples against PAAS show contrasting 491


<!-- Page 22 -->


patterns. Only one sample of the Acre Basin (Sample AC 38) plots in the shale field 492

(Fig. 9) whereas the remaining ten samples plot outside of the shale field suggesting 493

that the REE concentrations have been perturbed by post-depositional processes 494

(Fig. 9). The AC 22A show strong enrichment in HREE (Fig. 9). This strong HREE 495

enrichment could be associated with a primary phase of the pedologic process. In a 496

study of the lateritic process in a tropical environment, Viers and Wasserburg (2004) 497

indicated that the zircon dissolution could elevate the HREE concentrations at the 498

early stage of the weathering process, and the Zr precipitation could remove the REE 499

during that phase. This could explain the HREE enrichment for samples AC 22, 27A, 500

and 38. The remaining samples (AC 15A, 42B, 30A, 20A2, 37, and 49) show 501

enrichment in LREE over HREE and plot between the “shales” and “seawater” fields 502

in Fig. 9. 503

The Madre de Dios samples have a high Al/Si ratio which ranges between 504

0.33 and 0.44 (except for MD-2019-11E, Al/Si = 0.23), which suggests that are fine 505

and clay-rich sediments (Bouchez et al., 2011) (Table 3, Fig. 9). The lack of 506

correlation (see in the supplementary dataset) between CIA and Al/Si with REE 507

content, Eu/Eu*, Cr/Th, and ƐNd (0) values implies that the provenance indicators 508

have not been altered by chemical weathering and sedimentary sorting. The samples 509

exhibit low Eu/Eu* ratios (Table 3) indicating that diagenetic remobilization of Eu was 510

insignificant in our samples. The Madre de Dios samples have more uniform major 511

and trace elements and REE concentration patterns when compared with those of 512

the Acre Basin (Figs. 5A and 5B). The analyzed samples from Madre de Dios exhibit 513

Ce anomalies (ΩCe) above 0.85 and display flat REE patterns when compared to 514

PAAS, indicating their classification within “shales” field (Fig. 9). This characteristic, 515


<!-- Page 23 -->


typical of continental clays (see Moiroud et al., (2016), suggest that these samples 516

are unaffected  by marine autogenesis. 517

5.2. Interpretation of provenance 518

The Th/Sc, Cr/Th elemental ratios and the Eu/Eu* ratios of the Acre Basin 519

samples are in favor of a silicic/felsic source sensu Cullers (2000) source: the Th/Sc 520

is between 0. and 4.5; the Cr/Th ratios are equal or higher than 1.0 and the Eu/Eu* 521

ratios are between 0.50 - 0.65. This is also the case for the analyzed Madre de Dios 522

sedimentary rocks with Th/Sc ratio range (0.64 - 0.87); Cr/Th ratio (between 5.14 and 523

7.23), and Eu/Eu* values (0.59 and 0.67 (Table 3, Fig. 8) characteristics of 524

silicic/felsic sources (Cullers, 2000). Further insights can be obtained by considering 525

the Nd isotopic composition of the analyzed samples, which can provide additional 526

constrains. 527

Therefore, the Nd isotopic compositions observed in sedimentary rocks from 528

the Andean and Amazonian regions can be attributed to a combination between 529

juvenile primitive Andean Arc and older cratonic sources (Basu et al., 1990; Roddaz 530

et al., 2005). Cratonic sedimentary rocks are characterized by negative ƐNd (0) 531

values, between -14.5 and -20, and Nd model ages (TDM) from 1.75 to 3.3 Ga, while 532

Andean-derived sediments have more positive ƐNd (0) values and TDM lower than 1.6 533

Ga (Cordani & Sato, 1999; Figueiredo et al., 2009; Carina Hoorn et al., 2017; Horbe 534

et al., 2013; Roddaz et al., 2005). Within Colombia, a threshold value of -12.7 for 535

εNd(0) has been employed to differentiate sedimentary rocks derived from the 536

Andean or cratonic sources  (Nie et al., 2012). Similarly, zircon U-Pb ages have been 537

used in provenance studies of Amazonian sediments to decipher the relative 538

contributions of Andean and cratonic source rocks (Erlich et al., 2018; George et al., 539

2019; Gutiérrez et al., 2019; Horton, 2018; Hurtado et al., 2018; Louterbach et al., 540


<!-- Page 24 -->


2018; Moreno et al., 2020; Perez et al., 2016). The distinct geological ages of the 541

Andean Cordillera and the Amazon craton account for their compositional 542

differences. For instance, the Amazon craton is defined by Precambrian zircon U–Pb 543

ages (>600 Ma, Fig. 3) (Bahlburg et al., 2009; Chew et al., 2008; Chew et al., 2007; 544

Cordani et al., 2000; Cordani & Sato, 1999; Rizzotto & Quadros, 2005; Santos et al., 545

2000; Tassinari & Macambira, 1999). In contrast, the Andes are mostly characterized 546

by Phanerozoic zircon U-Pb ages (<550 Ma, mainly Mesozoic-Cenozoic ages, Fig. 3) 547

(DeCelles et al., 2011; Horton et al., 2016; Martin-Gombojav & Winkler, 2008; Nie et 548

al., 2012; Perez et al., 2016), except for the Marañón Complex which crops out in the 549

Peruvian Eastern Cordillera. The Marañón complex is composed of metamorphic and 550

plutonic rocks of the Precambrian age (Chew et al., 2007; Ramos & Folguera, 2009). 551

Except for the three youngest samples of the Campanian-Maastrichtian 552

Divisor Formation (AC 20 A2, AC 16, and AC 15A) that could have been perturbed 553

by pedogenetic processes, the ƐNd (0) values together with the TDM ages of other 554

analyzed samples of the Acre Basin (Table 4) suggest that sedimentary rocks were 555

sourced from cratonic rocks. When compared with the Cretaceous sedimentary rocks 556

of the Huallaga Basin (Hurtado et al., 2018), they have similar negative ƐNd (0) values 557

as those of the Cenomanian (Agua Caliente Formation - HUA 245), Coniacian- 558

Turonian (Chonta Formation - HUA 240 and 244) and Maastrichtian (Vivian 559

Formation - HUA 462). 560

The U-Pb zircon age distribution of Cenomanian to Maastrichtian samples of 561

the Acre Basin also suggests a cratonic source with a dominant population of zircon 562

aged between 1.8 and 2.0 Ga related to the tectonic province of Ventuari-Tapajos 563

(2.0-1.82 Ga). The sample HUA 462 of the Huallaga Basin  (Hurtado et al., 2018), 564


<!-- Page 25 -->


some samples of the Marañón Basin (Chonta 22-06-08-04; Chonta Palo Seco-1X – 565

2299m; Lower Vivian 20-06-08-19; Lower Vivian #120 Pagoreni 1003-ST1; Upper 566

Vivian #62 Yarina-2X.; Erlich et al., 2018), the early Maastrichtian sample of the 567

Madre de Dios Basin (MD 239, Louterbach et al., 2018) and the sample (SG1616) 568

analyzed in George et al. (2019) also present zircons aged between 1.82 and 2.0 Ga 569

(Venturi-Tapajos), which suggest a common source. The second dominant 570

The sample HUA 266A of the Huallaga Basin (in Hurtado et al., 2018) and some 573

samples (Chonta #141 Tuncheplaya-95X 3201m; Chonta Palo Seco-1X – 2299m; 574
